studies.applyIt: Notice what you do with your appearance today that is aimed at strangers rather than at the people you live with. Not in order to change it. This ayah spends most of its length describing the household where none of this applies, and that proportion is worth sitting with for a few minutes.

studies.title: If They Are Poor
studies.meaning: After a long passage on restraint, the surah turns to provision. Marriages are to be arranged for those in the community without partners, and the objection anyone would raise is answered before it is voiced: if they are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty. Poverty is named as the obstacle, which tells us what was actually preventing such matches. The ayah closes on two names, one for God's amplitude and one for His knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators note that this ayah follows the passages on restraint deliberately, since a community asked to guard against one thing is here given the means for another. The economic point is specific: marriage in Medina required bridewealth and a household, and the poor among the community, including many recent emigrants, had neither.

keyTerms.note: A plural covering the unmarried, the widowed and the divorced together, of both sexes. It occurs once in the Quran, and its breadth lets one word address several very different situations.
From the root for being free of need, the same root as one of the divine names. The verb says God removes the lack rather than supplying a subsidy, which is a different claim entirely.
From a root for breadth and room. Applied to God it names capacity without limit, and it answers the assumption behind the objection, which is that resources are a fixed quantity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marriage was expensive. Bridewealth was paid to the woman herself, a household had to be set up, and a young man without means could wait years or never marry at all. Communities accumulated unmarried people for purely economic reasons, and everyone knew exactly who they were. This ayah addresses the families and guardians who arranged such matters rather than the individuals waiting.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for those without a spouse occurs only once in the Quran, and it covers the never-married, the widowed and the divorced in a single term without distinguishing men from women. Arabic has separate words for each of those states, so choosing one that erases every distinction is a deliberate move.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a communal responsibility out of something usually treated as private fortune. It also answers an economic objection with a theological claim, which is a risky move, and it does so without promising wealth: what is named is the removal of need rather than the arrival of plenty. Provision is presented as following a step taken rather than as something to be waited for first.

crossReferences.why: Names the bridewealth given to the woman herself, which is the cost this ayah anticipates.
States that God provides from where a person does not expect, and suffices whoever relies.
Contrasts a whispered promise of poverty with God's promise of forgiveness and bounty.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good thing you have postponed until the money is right: a marriage, a move, a commitment. Ask honestly how much of the delay is arithmetic and how much is fear wearing arithmetic's clothes. This ayah answers a financial objection with a claim about God, and telling the two apart is the first step.

studies.title: Seeking The Goods Of This Life
studies.meaning: Three situations are handled in one long ayah, and one concern runs through all of them. Those without the means to marry hold to restraint until God provides. Those in servitude who seek a written contract for their freedom are to be granted it where good is recognised in them, and given from God's wealth toward the sum. And compelling a woman under one's authority into sexual exploitation for worldly gain is shut off, with mercy named for the one compelled.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators describe a practice in pre-Islamic Arabia in which owners profited from women they held, and report that this ayah addressed cases raised in Medina. The written contract named here was a recognised instrument by which an enslaved person purchased their own freedom in instalments, and the ayah turns it from an owner's option into something to be granted.

keyTerms.note: A verb form implying two parties writing to each other, so the arrangement is mutual rather than conferred downward. It occurs once in the Quran, naming a contract the person seeking freedom initiates.
A word for something offered and quickly gone, used throughout the Quran of worldly advantage. Naming the motive this way measures the profit against what it costs another person.
From the root for a fortress, the same root behind the word for women of protected honour earlier in this surah. The desire named is for one's own protection, and the ayah makes it decisive.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Slavery in Arabia was ordinary and everywhere, and an enslaved person had no route out except an owner's goodwill. The written contract was that route: a sum agreed, paid in instalments out of earnings, with freedom at the end. This ayah names it, tells those holding wealth to contribute toward it, and so converts a private favour into a public expectation.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb naming this contract occurs once in the Quran, and its form implies both parties writing, so the arrangement is described as mutual rather than as something handed down. The word for the worldly gain that motivates the compulsion in the last clause is one the Quran uses repeatedly for what is fleeting, set here directly against a person's wish for protection.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah moves from restraint by the poor, to freedom for the enslaved, to protection for the coerced, and each step transfers something from those with power to those with less. The final clause is the most striking: mercy is named for the one who was compelled rather than for the one compelling, which locates the guilt precisely where the coercion began.

crossReferences.why: Names the freeing of a person as the first item on the steep path few undertake.
Lists the freeing of those in bondage among the purposes charity is gathered for.
Uses the same word for women held in a household, in a passage about marrying them.

studies.applyIt: Look at one arrangement you benefit from where the other person has less room to walk away than you do: an employee, a tenant, a favour long overdue. Ask what you would do differently if they could leave freely. This ayah keeps moving in one direction, and that question shows you where you stand in it.

studies.title: Three Things Sent Down
studies.meaning: Three things are named as having been sent down, and they differ in kind. Clarifying signs, an example drawn from those who passed away before, and counsel for those who are mindful. The list moves from statement to story to exhortation, which is roughly the three ways the Quran works on a reader. The ayah sits between the passage on the community's failures and the passage on light, and it functions as a hinge between them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed immediately before the surah's most famous passage. Commentators read this ayah as closing the section on conduct and opening the section on light, since the phrase about clarifying signs recurs twelve ayat later and brackets the whole stretch between the two. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for it.

keyTerms.note: An active participle, so the signs are described as doing the clarifying rather than as being clear themselves. That is a different claim: they work on the reader instead of merely presenting well.
A word covering both a parable and a case that stands in for others. Applied to earlier peoples it names history used as illustration rather than history kept as record.
From the same root as the verb used earlier in this surah for God counselling the community after the slander. It names speech aimed at the heart rather than at the understanding.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Instruction in that world came in exactly these three forms. A judgement was stated, an ancestor's fate was recalled, and an elder said something short that stayed with you for years. Poetry carried all three, often inside the same ode. An audience hearing this list would recognise it as the shape of how anything worth passing on was actually passed on.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about clarifying signs being sent down occurs three times in the Quran, and two of them are in this surah, twelve ayat apart. Between the two sits the passage on light and its opposite, so the surah encloses its most famous material inside a repeated frame that says the material has been made plain.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah describes revelation as working through three channels at once, and it does not rank them. A statement, a story and a word of counsel are given equal standing, which resists reducing scripture to doctrine. Naming counsel last, and directing it at those already mindful, also concedes that the third kind lands only on someone already inclined to hear it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the phrase about clarifying signs, closing the frame this ayah opens.
Names the accounts of earlier peoples as a lesson for those who understand.
Calls the revelation counsel from your Lord and a healing for what is in the breasts.

studies.applyIt: Notice which of the three you actually respond to: a plain statement, a story about someone, or a short line that lodges in you. People differ, and most of us keep reaching for the one that works least. Try the other two on something you have been avoiding, and see which one moves you.

studies.title: Light Upon Light
studies.meaning: The ayah opens with a statement and then does not explain it. God is the Light of the heavens and the earth, and what follows is offered as a likeness of His light rather than of Him. The image is built by narrowing: a niche, a lamp inside it, glass around the lamp, the glass like a shining star, oil from an olive tree that belongs to no side of the hill and almost gives light untouched by fire. The commentators read the parts variously and record the range.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a surah otherwise occupied with households, privacy and public conduct, which makes the sudden appearance of this ayah striking. It comes immediately before a description of houses where God's name is remembered morning and evening. The classical sources report no specific occasion. The surah takes its name from this ayah, and its placement among ordinary domestic instructions is part of how it reads.

keyTerms.note: A recess cut into a wall to hold a lamp, closed at the back so the light is thrown forward rather than dispersed. The word occurs once in the Quran and describes a household fitting everyone recognised.
An adjective connected by the commentators either to pearls or to the verb for driving away darkness. The readings differ, and both give the same picture: a light that does not flicker.

The commentators read this of a tree standing where the sun reaches it all day rather than only morning or afternoon, which was known to make the best oil. Others read it as belonging to no place at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every part of the image was household equipment. A niche in the wall held the lamp because a shelf spilled the light; glass around a wick kept it from guttering and doubled the brightness; olive oil was the fuel that burned cleanest and cost most. Anyone in that room could check the description against the lamp beside them. The parable is made entirely of things within arm's reach.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah is one of the most commented on in the whole Quran, and entire books have been written on it alone. The word for the niche appears nowhere else in the text. It has also shaped Islamic architecture: the niche in a mosque wall and the lamps hung before it are a deliberate echo of this image, repeated across a thousand years of building.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah is careful about what it compares. God is named as Light directly, but the parable is introduced as the likeness of His light, not of Him, and every classical commentator holds that line. What the image does is describe light that is contained without being diminished and given without being consumed. The oil almost shining before any fire touches it is the detail most often dwelt on, and it suggests a readiness that precedes the kindling.

crossReferences.why: What the parable is placed next to: houses where God's name is remembered daily.
Describes a chest opened to submission, carrying a light from its Lord.
Shows the light running ahead of believers on the Day, and others asking for some.

studies.applyIt: Turn off every light in one room tonight and light a single candle, then sit with it for two minutes. Notice how much it lights and how far the edge of it reaches. The ayah is built entirely from a lamp in a room, and it was written for people who had actually looked at one. Look at one.

studies.title: Trade That Does Not Distract
studies.meaning: The lamp of the previous ayah is now located: in houses God has permitted to be raised, where His name is remembered and He is glorified morning and late afternoon. Then the people are described, and the description works by negation. Men whom trade and selling do not draw away from remembrance, prayer and giving. They are not people without business. They are people whose business does not get to name the hour.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators read the houses as places of worship generally, and some read them more widely as any home where God's name is kept alive. Medina's mosque stood beside its market, so the two activities these ayat set against each other happened within earshot of one another. No specific occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.gloss: to be raised, to be honoured
keyTerms.note: A verb covering both physical building and elevation in standing. The commentators read both senses, so the houses are described as constructed and as held high at the same time.
From a root for diversion and amusement. It does not mean prevented but drawn away, so the failure it names is attention going elsewhere rather than a choice being made.
A plural for the hours between afternoon and sunset, when the heat breaks and work winds down. It occurs three times in the Quran, and always paired with the morning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina's market ran on a rhythm everybody knew: goods arrived, prices moved, and the hour a caravan unloaded was the hour money was made. Missing it cost real money. The men described here are not withdrawing from that world, and the passage is careful to say so. They are inside it and still leaving the stall when the call comes.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the late afternoon hours in this passage occurs three times in the Quran and is always paired with the morning, never standing alone. The verb describing hearts and eyes turning over in the following line occurs in this form once, and it belongs to a root used elsewhere for turning an object over in the hand.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage defines devotion by what it survives rather than by what it renounces. Trade is not criticised; distraction is. That places the test inside ordinary working life instead of outside it, and it makes the relevant quality attention rather than austerity. Naming the fear of a day of overturning at the end supplies the reason such attention is possible at all.

crossReferences.why: Describes a congregation leaving the gathering for a passing caravan, the same tension.
Warns that wealth and children can divert people from the remembrance of God.
Uses the same pairing of morning and late afternoon for remembering your Lord.

studies.applyIt: Pick the hour of your day when stopping costs you most, and stop for four minutes inside it. Not before it, not after. This passage is not about people with less to do; it is about people whose work does not get to name the hour. One deliberate interruption will tell you where you actually stand.

studies.title: Rewarded For Their Best
studies.meaning: The reward is described with a precision easy to miss. God repays them according to the best of what they did, not the average and not the total. Then He increases them from His bounty, which is a second and separate act. The closing clause widens further still: God provides for whom He wills without reckoning. Three stages, and each one loosens the arithmetic more than the last.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the description of those who keep God's name alive in the houses raised for it. Commentators read the phrase about the best of what they did as the whole record being valued at its highest point, and they note the deliberate move from measured recompense to unmeasured giving across the two halves of the ayah.

keyTerms.gloss: the best of, the finest of
keyTerms.note: A superlative, so the standard applied is a person's peak rather than their average. The ayah leaves the ordinary and the poor parts of a record out of the calculation entirely.
A verb for adding beyond what was there. It arrives after the reward has already been described, so the increase is not part of the settlement but something following it.
A phrase denying that the giving is counted at all. It can mean without limit or without being called to account, and the commentators keep both readings side by side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in that economy was weighed and counted. Grain was measured in known volumes, silver by weight, debts recorded by witness, and a merchant's reputation rested on the accuracy of his scales. The Quran uses that vocabulary constantly. A phrase saying something is given without any reckoning would have sounded, to that audience, close to a description of carelessness.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about God giving without reckoning occurs seven times across the Quran, in settings as different as the adornment of this world's life, Mary finding provision waiting for her in the sanctuary, and the wealth granted to a king who was told to give or withhold freely. The same formula travels across quite different kinds of gift.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah dismantles the idea of a proportional settlement in three moves. First the record is valued at its best, then something is added, then the adding is described as uncounted. What survives is the notion that God repays; what is removed is any way of predicting the sum. That leaves effort meaningful and calculation impossible at the same time.

crossReferences.why: States that their worst deeds are removed and they are repaid for the best they did.
Multiplies a single act of spending sevenfold and then further, for whom He wills.
Uses the same phrase about provision without reckoning, found in a sanctuary.

studies.applyIt: Think of the best thing you did this year, the single best. Now notice how rarely it comes to mind compared with your failures. This ayah describes a reckoning that takes the peak rather than the average, and holding that in view for one afternoon is a different way of looking back.

studies.title: A Mirage On Flat Ground
studies.meaning: The image is exact. A mirage on level open ground, taken for water by someone thirsty, who reaches it and finds nothing at all. Then the sentence turns: he finds God there instead, and his account is settled in full. The parable's point is not that the works were worthless but that they were never what they appeared to be. And the disappointment is not the end of the scene, since something is waiting where the water was not.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening the pair of comparisons that answer the passage on light. Commentators note that the two images which follow, a desert mirage and a dark sea, cover the two landscapes the audience knew as most disorienting. No specific occasion is reported, and the parables are read as describing a type rather than named individuals.

keyTerms.note: The shimmer of heated air read as water. The word occurs twice in the Quran, here and of mountains dissolving on the last day, so both uses concern something solid proving unreal.
A word for flat land with no feature to break it. It occurs once in the Quran, and the flatness matters, since a mirage needs an unobstructed plain to appear at all.
A single word for a person in the grip of thirst. It occurs once in the Quran, and it explains the misperception, because thirst is what makes a shimmer readable as water.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mirages were a known hazard rather than a poetic image. A traveller who left the route to chase water that was not there could die of the detour, and guides warned about them the way sailors warn about rocks. Everyone in the audience had either seen one or been told what to do about it, which was to keep to the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a mirage occurs twice in the Quran. Its other use describes mountains on the last day, set in motion until they become a mirage, so the same word covers a person's works and the most solid thing in a landscape. Two further words in this ayah occur nowhere else in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The parable takes aim at what a thing was, not at how hard someone tried. A person reaching a mirage has genuinely walked, and the walking was real; what was not real was the destination. That distinguishes this from an image of laziness. And the ending refuses the obvious close, since instead of emptiness God is found there, which turns futility into arrival.

crossReferences.why: Turns their deeds into scattered dust, the same result reached by a different image.
Compares deeds to ashes blown apart by the wind on a stormy day.
Names those whose effort went astray while they thought they were doing well.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are working hard at because of what you expect at the end of it. Then ask what you would still do if the end were removed. Most answers are uncomfortable and none of them require action today. This parable is about walking toward something, and it only asks what.

studies.title: Darkness Upon Darkness
studies.meaning: The second image stacks obstruction in layers. A deep sea, covered by a wave, above it another wave, above that cloud: darknesses one on top of another. Then a detail that makes it physical rather than abstract, that a man putting out his hand would scarcely see it. The closing clause states the principle plainly, that whoever God has given no light has none. This is the exact counterweight to light upon light.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the pair of comparisons that follow the passage on light. Commentators note the deliberate symmetry, since the surah has described light upon light and now describes darkness upon darkness. The sea imagery is unusual for this audience and is read as drawing on what traders working the Red Sea routes could describe from experience.

keyTerms.note: An adjective from a root for depth and for the roar of a crowd. It names water far from any coast, where nothing can be reached by wading and no bottom is available underfoot.
A plural that English cannot easily carry. Darkness is treated here as a countable thing which can be stacked, which is why the ayah can describe some of it as lying above other parts.
A verb for something spreading across a surface and hiding what lies under it. Repeating the structure three times builds the layers without ever using a word for adding.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab traders knew the Red Sea and the routes toward India, and sailors' accounts of a night storm far from land circulated in Mecca and Medina as travellers' talk. Very few in the audience had been there. The image would have worked on them roughly as an account of deep ocean works on most people now: vivid, secondhand, and frightening.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah is built as the mirror of the light passage a few ayat earlier. That one ends with the phrase light upon light; this one carries darkness upon darkness at its centre. The surah takes its name from the first of the two, so the chapter is named for the half of the pair that describes what is given rather than what is withheld.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the absence of guidance outside a person's reach rather than inside their reasoning. The man in the image is not refusing to see; there is nothing to see by. That is a hard statement and the ayah does not soften it. What it establishes is that seeing depends on something given, which makes the light of the earlier passage a gift rather than an achievement.

crossReferences.why: Carries the matching image, ending with the phrase this ayah inverts at its centre.
Describes someone given a light to walk among people, set against one left in darkness.
Names God as bringing believers out of darknesses into light, using the same plural.

studies.applyIt: Sit in a genuinely dark room for two minutes and hold your hand up in front of your face. This ayah describes precisely that gesture. Most people have never actually tested it, and the point is not fear but scale: how completely ordinary confidence depends on something you did not supply.

studies.title: Each Knows Its Own Praise
studies.meaning: A question opens onto a claim easy to read past. Everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies God, and the birds with wings spread are named separately. Then the striking clause: each one has known its own prayer and its own glorification. Not a shared liturgy but a form particular to each creature, already known to it. The second ayah closes with ownership and return, placing the whole arrangement inside what belongs to God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the stretch of the surah that argues from what can be observed. Commentators discuss whether the knowing in the final clause belongs to the creatures or to God, and record both readings without resolving them. The birds are singled out, which the classical readers connect to their being visible overhead to anyone who happens to look up.

keyTerms.note: A verb from a root for swimming or moving freely through something. Glorification in this sense is a motion away from any defect rather than a particular form of words.
A participle for holding in a row or a line. Used of birds it describes wings held out and steady rather than beating, which is the posture of gliding on a current.
The ordinary word for prayer, attached here to a bird or a creature. That extension is the ayah's most surprising move, and the commentators note it rather than explaining it away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Birds were watched closely and read for meaning. Their direction was taken as an omen before Islam, flocks marked water and weather, and anyone travelling watched the sky as a matter of course. This ayah takes a habit of observation the audience already had and redirects it, so what a bird indicates is not a fortune but a form of worship.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for birds holding their wings spread in rank occurs three times in the Quran. One other use opens a surah with an oath by those drawn up in ranks, and the third describes birds overhead held up by nothing but the Merciful. The same participle therefore covers birds, ranks, and the act of standing in line.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Assigning each creature its own prayer, already known to it, makes worship a feature of creation rather than a human institution. That reframes the human position, since a person praying is joining something already underway rather than beginning it. And the knowing is put in the past tense, so nothing has to be taught, which locates each creature's worship in how it was made.

crossReferences.why: States that everything glorifies God, though you do not understand their glorification.
Uses the same word for birds with wings spread, held up by the Merciful alone.
Describes everything in the heavens and earth prostrating, along with their shadows.

studies.applyIt: Watch one bird for a full minute today, until you notice something you would not have guessed. This ayah says the creature already knows its own form of worship, which is not a claim you can verify. But the watching is the part available to you, and a minute is longer than it sounds.

studies.title: Mountains Of Hail
studies.meaning: A sequence is traced rather than a result announced. God drives the clouds, then joins them, then piles them into a mass, and the rain is seen emerging from the gaps within it. Then hail is described as coming down from mountains in the sky, reaching some and turned away from others. The ayah ends with lightning whose flash nearly takes the sight away. Every stage is something a person standing outside can watch happen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's run of ayat arguing from observation. Commentators note that this passage and those around it each open with the same question, do you not see, and read them as one continuous argument. The description of hail is unusual in the Quran, and the sources treat the whole sequence as a single sustained look at weather.

keyTerms.note: A verb for pushing something forward slowly, used of driving animals. Applied to clouds it describes a slow herding rather than a wind blowing, which is what a sky before rain looks like.
A word for something piled up in layers. It occurs once in the Quran, and it names the stage between scattered cloud and falling rain, which is a genuinely observable moment.
A specific word for rain coming out of cloud rather than for rainfall in general. It occurs twice in the Quran, both times inside an account of clouds being gathered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain was watched with an attention hard to imagine now. People read cloud shape and direction to know whether water would fall on their valley or the next one, and being wrong meant moving herds for nothing. Hail was known and destructive, capable of stripping a crop in minutes. The selective language here, reaching some and turned from others, described something everyone had lived through.
studies.didYouKnow: The specific word this ayah uses for rain emerging from cloud occurs twice in the Quran, and both occurrences sit inside accounts of clouds being driven, joined and heaped, describing the same stages in the same order. The word for the heaped mass itself occurs once in the whole text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes its case from process rather than from origin. What is offered is not the fact that rain exists but the sequence by which it arrives, each step named and each step visible. That treats attention as the route to the conclusion. The selective clause, reaching some and turned from others, then introduces will into a description of weather, which is where the argument lands.

crossReferences.why: Traces the same stages of cloud and rain, using the same specific word for the fall.
Joins lightning to fear and hope, and to the raising of the heavy clouds.
Uses a storm's darkness, thunder and lightning as an image for those who reject.

studies.applyIt: The next time it rains where you are, watch the sky for two minutes before it starts rather than after. The gathering is the part this ayah describes and the part nobody looks at. It is free, it happens often, and it is the whole of the argument being made here.

studies.title: Every Creature From Water
studies.meaning: Two short ayat, and the second is the surprising one. God turns the night and the day over, which is offered as a lesson for those with sight. Then: God created every moving creature from water, and they are sorted by how they move, on the belly, on two feet, on four. The classification is by gait rather than by kind, which is an unusual way to divide the living world, and it closes by saying God creates what He wills.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the run of ayat arguing from observation. Commentators read the three ways of moving as illustrative rather than exhaustive, since the final clause explicitly leaves room for more. No specific occasion is reported, and the passage is treated as part of the surah's turn away from conduct and toward creation.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for flipping something repeatedly, used of turning an object over in the hand. The same root appeared a few ayat earlier for hearts turning over on the last day.
From a root meaning to cross from one side to the other. A lesson in this sense is something you pass through, from the visible to the meaning, which is why it is offered to those with sight.
From the verb to walk or creep. The word names anything that moves upon the earth, which is why the ayah can then classify by gait without leaving anything outside the list.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water defined everything. A settlement existed because of a well, herds were moved between them, and the value of land was the value of its access. The claim that every living thing was made from water was not a laboratory statement to that audience. It matched the most basic observed fact of their lives: where water was, life was, and where it stopped, life did.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage sorts living creatures by how they move rather than by what they are, naming three gaits in ascending order of legs and then adding that God creates what He wills, which leaves the list open. The verb for turning night and day over shares its root with the verb used a few ayat earlier for hearts turning over.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Setting a single origin, water, beside a variety of forms makes difference secondary to shared substance. The classification underlines it, since creatures that could hardly be more unlike are separated only by gait. And the open ending, that God creates what He wills, keeps the list from hardening into a taxonomy, so the passage describes an order without claiming to have finished describing it.

crossReferences.why: States that every living thing was made from water, in a passage about sky and earth.
Names water as what a human being was created from, then made into kin and marriage.
Names the alternation of night and day as a sign for those with understanding.

studies.applyIt: Name three creatures you have seen this week and how each of them moved. Most people cannot do it, because we file animals by what they are rather than by what they do. This passage sorts them the other way, and doing the same for ten minutes changes what you notice on the walk home.

studies.title: We Obey, And Then Turn
studies.meaning: The frame closes with the phrase that opened it: clarifying signs have been sent down, and God guides whom He wills to a straight path. Then a portrait. They say we believe in God and the Messenger and we obey, and afterwards a group of them turns away. The verdict is short and flat, that those are not believers. What is being described is not doubt but a gap between what is said and what follows it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators connect these ayat to people in Medina whose formal adherence was not matched by their conduct, particularly when disputes were brought for judgement. The surah has already described a whole community failing under pressure, and this passage narrows from that failure to a specific kind of person, without naming individuals.

keyTerms.note: A verb of compliance set in the past tense, so the claim concerns a record rather than an intention. The following clause then contradicts it with a later action, which is why the verdict is so brief.

keyTerms.gloss: a party, a portion of them
keyTerms.note: A word for a group split off from a larger one. Its use keeps the charge from covering everyone who made the statement, a care the passage shows throughout.
From a root for turning and also for taking charge of something. Turning away in Arabic is physical, describing a body rotating, so the word carries an image rather than an attitude.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public declarations mattered because there was nothing else. A person joined a community by saying so in front of witnesses, and there was no register, no card and no ceremony beyond the words. That made the gap between statement and behaviour the only measure available, and it made a group who said the right thing and acted otherwise a genuine practical problem.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about clarifying signs being sent down appears twice in this surah, and this is the second, twelve ayat after the first. The whole passage on light, darkness, birds, clouds, night and day, and the origin of living creatures sits between them, so the surah's central material is framed on both sides by the same claim.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage judges by sequence rather than by statement. What disqualifies is not the absence of a declaration but what happens after it, which places belief in a stretch of time rather than in a moment. And the verdict is delivered as description rather than as accusation: they are not believers, stated as a fact about a category, which is how the Quran usually handles this.

crossReferences.why: Distinguishes saying we have believed from faith having actually entered the heart.
Describes people saying they believe in God and the Last Day while they do not.
Records a declaration made with the tongue that the next clause immediately denies.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you said out loud that you have not done. Not a lie, just a stated intention that quietly lapsed. Name one, and either do it this week or say plainly that you are not going to. This passage is about the distance between a sentence and what follows it, and closing one is enough.

studies.title: They Come Willingly Enough
studies.meaning: The behaviour is described with a precision that makes it instantly recognisable. Called to God and His Messenger for judgement, a group of them turns aside. But if the right is on their side, they come submissively. The two ayat sit together so that the second exposes the first. What looked like a principled objection to the process turns out to be a calculation about the outcome, and nothing has to be said about motive.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage about people whose declared adherence outran their conduct. Commentators connect these ayat to disputes in Medina where one party preferred an arbitration likely to favour them, and they read the pairing as a diagnosis rather than an accusation. The reports do not agree on particular cases, and the sources leave the matter general.

keyTerms.note: A participle from a root meaning to present one's side rather than one's face. It describes the physical posture of avoidance, someone facing away without leaving the room.
The same word used for truth and for reality throughout the Quran, here in its legal sense of a valid claim. The overlap is the point, since they accept the process only when reality favours them.
A participle used of a camel that submits to being led. It occurs once in the Quran, and its animal origin makes the compliance look eager rather than dignified.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration in Arabia was voluntary, and choosing your arbitrator was half the case. A party expecting to lose would find reasons to go elsewhere, and everyone understood the manoeuvre perfectly well. What is described here was therefore not unusual behaviour; it was standard practice, which is exactly why naming it in scripture had force.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing how they arrive when the case suits them occurs once in the Quran, and it comes from a term for a camel that yields to being led without resistance. Placed at the end of a two-ayah sequence about avoiding judgement, the image supplies the entire comment on the behaviour without a word of accusation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage establishes that submission to a process is only real while the outcome is unknown. Accepting a judgement that favours you is not acceptance of judgement at all. That is a general test, applicable well beyond its occasion, and the Quran states it by setting two behaviours side by side rather than by articulating a principle.

crossReferences.why: Gives the opposite response, hearing and obeying when called to judgement.
Ties belief to accepting a judgement without finding resistance within oneself.
Describes people claiming faith while seeking judgement somewhere other than they said.

studies.applyIt: Think of a process you complain about only when it goes against you: a referee, a committee, a rule at work. Notice whether your objection ever arrives on a day you won. This passage makes its whole case by placing two behaviours side by side, and you can run the same test on yourself in a minute.

studies.title: Do They Fear Injustice
studies.meaning: Three possibilities are put as questions, in ascending order of seriousness. Is there sickness in their hearts, or have they fallen into doubt, or do they fear that God and His Messenger will deal unfairly with them. The third is what the ayah is really asking, and it is answered at once: rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers. The accusation is turned around inside the same sentence that raised it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about those who avoided judgement when the outcome looked unfavourable. Commentators read the three questions as covering the three explanations available for such behaviour, and note that the ayah supplies its own answer rather than leaving the questions hanging. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for it.

keyTerms.note: A verb from the root for unsettled suspicion, describing doubt that has taken hold rather than a question being asked. The form suggests entering a state rather than holding an opinion.
From a root meaning to lean to one side, so injustice here is described as a scale tipping rather than as cruelty. The verb occurs once in the Quran.
A particle that cancels what precedes it and substitutes something else. Its use here dismisses all three possibilities at once and replaces them with a statement about the questioners.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The fear behind the third question was rational in that world. Arbitrators were human, related to somebody, and open to pressure, and a party with less standing genuinely could expect a tilted result. That expectation was then carried into a setting where the judgement being avoided was not a chief's. The ayah addresses the transfer directly, without dismissing where the fear came from.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for tilting a judgement unfairly occurs once in the Quran, and its root describes leaning to one side rather than any act of cruelty. The ayah puts three questions in a row and answers none of them, replacing all three with a single flat statement introduced by a particle whose entire function is to cancel what came before.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah names a suspicion people rarely state, which is that God's judgement might not be fair to them. Raising it as a possibility gives it a hearing before it is rejected. The rejection then comes by reversal rather than by argument, since the ones fearing injustice are identified as its source. That places the distortion in the observer rather than in the process observed.

crossReferences.why: States that God does not wrong by the weight of an atom, and multiplies what is good.
Shows a record that leaves nothing out, closing with the line that your Lord wrongs no one.
Says God does not wrong people at all, but that people wrong themselves.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you avoid asking a question because you suspect you will not like the answer. That avoidance usually presents itself as being busy. This ayah names the suspicion underneath a whole pattern of behaviour and answers it in four words, and naming your own version takes about as long.

studies.title: Security In Place Of Fear
studies.meaning: A promise with four parts and one condition. Those who believe and act well are promised succession on the earth as earlier peoples had it, the establishing of the way approved for them, and the exchange of their fear for security. Then the condition is stated in a present-tense clause: they worship Me, associating nothing with Me. The commentators note that the promise is addressed to a community rather than to individuals.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources place the ayah in a period when the community in Medina was still under threat and, according to several reports, slept armed. The promise of security in place of fear is heard against that. The reports vary in detail and some commentators leave the setting general. The ayah sits among instructions about obedience and about the messenger's responsibility being delivery alone.

keyTerms.note: From the root for coming after someone, the same root behind the word for a successor or deputy. What is promised is not ownership but a turn, which by definition ends and passes on.
A verb of setting something in a place so that it holds, used of putting a foundation down. It is about stability rather than expansion, which is a narrower promise than it first sounds.
From the same root as the words for faith and for trustworthiness. The connection is not accidental: to be secure and to have faith are described in Arabic by one family of words.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Security was not a feeling in seventh-century Arabia; it was a set of arrangements. A community had it when its caravans travelled unescorted, its herds grazed at a distance, and its people slept without a watch on the roof. Losing it meant living with weapons in reach. The exchange the ayah promises would have been measured by the audience in exactly those terms, not in reassurance.
studies.didYouKnow: The condition attached to the promise is expressed as a present-tense description rather than as a command: they worship Me, associating nothing with Me. Commentators read the grammar as significant, since it describes what such a community is already doing rather than what it must begin. The clause about earlier peoples also makes the promise a repetition rather than a novelty.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The promise is conditional and the condition is worship, not effort, numbers or strategy. That places the relation between a community's inner life and its outward circumstances at the centre, without claiming the connection is mechanical or immediate. The word for succession also builds in an expiry: a successor holds what someone else held before and someone else will hold after. Nothing here promises permanence, only a turn.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same promise from an earlier scripture, the earth to the righteous.
Moses tells his people the earth is God's, given to whom He wills among His servants.
Names the same pair of gifts, food after hunger and security after fear.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing you are most afraid of at the moment, in one sentence, and write it on a piece of paper. Then write underneath what you would do differently tomorrow if it were settled. Keep the paper. The ayah promises an exchange rather than a removal, and knowing what you would do with the security is the part you can prepare now.
